title: Identity governance and privileged access management
summary: Who should have access, and who said so: joiner-mover-leaver, access reviews, role mining, separation of duties, PAM vaults, bastions, PAWs, just-in-time admin, break-glass and non-human identities.
outcomes: Explain the identity, access and privileged access lifecycles, and trace every entitlement to a rule or an approved request
Design joiner, mover and leaver handling from an authoritative source, including SCIM deprovisioning and reconciliation
Run access reviews that remove access, and mine candidate roles while spotting the exceptions that matter

lessons.title: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance

blocks.md:
Picture a company with 5,000 people and 300 applications. Every person has an account in dozens of those applications, and every account carries permissions. Ana works in sales. Today Ana can read the customer database, export it, and also read payroll. The first two make sense. Nobody can say why Ana can read payroll.

The authentication course (a prereq) taught how a system proves *who* is asking. The access control course (also a prereq) taught how an application decides *whether this request* is allowed. This course asks a third question that sits above both: **should this access exist at all, today, and who decided that?** That question, asked continuously for every person and every machine, is **identity governance**.

Words used all course:

- **Identity**: a person or thing the organisation knows about, usually a record in a central directory.
- **Account**: that identity's record inside one system. One identity has many accounts.
- **Entitlement**: one specific right granted to an account, such as a group membership, an application role or a permission (the word means something one is entitled to).
- **Authoritative source**: the system whose record wins when two disagree. For employees it is usually the HR (human resources) system; Microsoft's docs call it the HCM (human capital management) system.
- **Provisioning**: creating accounts and granting entitlements; **deprovisioning** is removing them.
- **PAM** (privileged access management): the tools and processes for the accounts whose misuse could damage many users or systems at once, such as administrators.
- **JIT** (just-in-time) access: privileged rights switched on for one task and off again afterwards, instead of held all the time (lesson 11).

Microsoft's documentation for its governance product frames the job as four questions, and they work for any product or none:

1. Which identities should have access to which resources?
2. What are those identities doing with that access?
3. Are there organisational controls in place for managing access?
4. Can auditors verify that the controls are working effectively?

The same page splits the work into three lifecycles, which is also the map of this course: the **identity lifecycle** (people join, move and leave: lessons 2 and 3), the **access lifecycle** (requests, reviews, roles and conflicts: lessons 4 to 6) and the **privileged access lifecycle** (administrators, vaults, jump hosts, just-in-time access and emergency accounts: lessons 7 to 11). Lesson 12 adds identities that are not people, and lesson 13 measures the whole thing.

blocks.title: Where governance sits around the login you already know

scenes.caption: The HR record is the starting point: it says who works here, in which job, and until when. Governance turns that record into accounts and entitlements.
Provisioning pushes accounts from the directory into each application. The login you met in the authentication course happens here; governance decides what the account holds.
Ana holds payroll access that no rule or request explains. Governance exists to find and remove grants like this one.
Administrators take a separate, guarded path: PAM decides who may be an administrator, when, and records what they do.
Every decision leaves evidence, so the fourth question (can an auditor verify it?) has an answer.

blocks.md:
The standard most controls are written against is **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5**, *Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations*, from NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology). Controls have family codes: **AC** is Access Control, **PS** is Personnel Security, **IA** is Identification and Authentication.

Its control **AC-2, Account Management**, reads like this course's checklist. Among its items: define the account types allowed and prohibited; assign account managers; require approvals for requests to create accounts; create, enable, modify, disable and remove accounts according to policy; monitor account use; notify account managers when accounts are no longer required and when users are terminated or transferred; review accounts on a set frequency; and align account management with personnel termination and transfer processes.

blocks.code:
# Every grant answers: who, what, why (which rule or request), approved by whom
GRANTS = [
    {"who": "ana", "what": "crm:read",     "why": "role:sales",  "by": "policy"},
    {"who": "ana", "what": "crm:export",   "why": "REQ-311",     "by": "mgr:lee"},
    {"who": "ana", "what": "payroll:read", "why": None,          "by": None},
    {"who": "ben", "what": "db:admin",     "why": "REQ-207",     "by": "ben"},
]
HR = {"ana": "active", "ben": "active"}

for g in GRANTS:
    problems = []
    if HR.get(g["who"]) != "active":
        problems.append("no active HR record")
    if g["why"] is None:
        problems.append("no reason on file")
    if g["by"] == g["who"]:
        problems.append("approved own request")
    print(f'{g["who"]:4} {g["what"]:13} {"; ".join(problems) or "ok"}')

# output:
# ana  crm:read      ok
# ana  crm:export    ok
# ana  payroll:read  no reason on file
# ben  db:admin      approved own request
blocks.caption: Python. Each grant carries who, what, why and who approved it. Two of four fail: one has no reason, one was approved by the person who asked. Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
The script is tiny, but it is the core habit of governance: **every grant must be traceable** to a rule (Ana is in sales, so Ana gets the sales role) or to a request with a named approver (REQ-311, approved by Ana's manager). A grant that traces to neither is called an **unexplained** or **orphaned entitlement**, and it is exactly what an attacker or an auditor finds first.

Ben's line shows the second habit: the person who benefits from a grant must not be the one who approves it. Lesson 6 makes that rule precise as separation of duties.

Identity governance answers: should this access exist, who decided, and can we prove it? Every entitlement should trace to a rule or an approved request, and the authoritative record (usually HR) drives the rest.

A common misconception is that identity and access management means single sign-on. Single sign-on proves who is logging in, once. It says nothing about whether Ana should still hold payroll access three jobs later. Governance works on the access itself, over time.

blocks.question: Which of these is an identity governance question rather than an authentication or per-request authorization question?
options: Did this login present a valid passkey for ana@corp.example?
Should Ana, who moved from finance to sales in March, still hold the payments role?
May the request GET /invoices/1002 return invoice 1002 to user 7?
Has this session cookie expired?
blocks.explain: Governance asks whether an entitlement should exist at all, over time. The passkey check and cookie expiry are authentication and session questions; the invoice check is the per-request authorization decision from the access control course.

blocks.question: In the script, Ben's db:admin grant was approved by Ben. Why is that a finding even though a request exists?
options: Because database access should never be requested
Because a request without a ticket number is invalid
Because the person who benefits approved it, so no second person ever judged the need
Because admin rights can only be granted by HR
blocks.explain: An approval is a second person's judgment. When the requester approves their own request, the record looks complete but no independent check happened. This is the core of separation of duties (lesson 6).

lessons.title: Joiner, mover, leaver: the lifecycle and how access creeps

blocks.md:
Every person's access has a life. Microsoft's lifecycle workflow documentation names its three phases, and the names are now standard across the industry:

- **Joiner**: someone enters the scope of needing access, such as a new employee.
- **Mover**: someone moves between boundaries inside the organisation, such as from marketing to sales. The move might need more access, or different access.
- **Leaver**: someone leaves the scope of needing access, for example by retiring or being terminated. Their access must be removed.

These events usually start in the HR system: a hire date, a department change, an end date. Lifecycle tools watch those attributes; Microsoft's example workflow emails a manager seven days before a new employee's `employeeHireDate`.

**Joiners** get two kinds of access. **Birthright access** is what everyone in a population gets automatically: email, the wiki, the expense tool. **Role-based access** comes from the job, using the RBAC (role-based access control) you met in the access control course: sales people get the sales role. The goal Microsoft states is that people are ready to work on day one, with nothing more than the job needs: least privilege from the start.

**Movers** are where most organisations quietly fail. NIST SP 800-53 control **PS-5, Personnel Transfer**, asks the organisation to review and confirm ongoing need for current access when someone is reassigned, and to modify access to match. The easy implementation only adds the new department's access. The old access stays. Do that three times and you get **privilege creep**: a long-serving employee who holds the access of every job they ever had.

blocks.title: Ana changes jobs twice: add-only versus desired state

scenes.caption: Ana joins marketing: birthright email and wiki, plus the marketing role (cms, ads). Both methods agree: 4 entitlements.
Ana moves to sales. Add-only grants crm and quotes and removes nothing (6). Desired state recomputes from HR: it adds crm and quotes and removes cms and ads (4).
Ana moves to finance. Add-only now holds all 8, including quotes (create quotes) and pay (approve payments) together. Desired state holds the 4 the finance job needs.

blocks.code:
BIRTHRIGHT = {"email", "wiki"}                      # every employee
ROLE_ACCESS = {"marketing": {"cms", "ads"},
               "sales":     {"crm", "quotes"},
               "finance":   {"ledger", "pay"}}

# WRONG: each change only ADDS the new department's access
def apply_change_additive(current, dept):
    return current | ROLE_ACCESS[dept]

# RIGHT: recompute desired state from the HR record, then diff
def desired(dept):
    return BIRTHRIGHT | ROLE_ACCESS[dept]

def apply_change_desired(current, dept):
    want = desired(dept)
    return want, sorted(want - current), sorted(current - want)

history = ["marketing", "sales", "finance"]       # Ana's three jobs
acc = desired(history[0])
for dept in history[1:]:
    acc = apply_change_additive(acc, dept)
print("additive:", sorted(acc), len(acc))

acc = desired(history[0])
for dept in history[1:]:
    acc, add, remove = apply_change_desired(acc, dept)
    print(f"to {dept}: add {add} remove {remove}")
print("desired: ", sorted(acc), len(acc))

# output:
# additive: ['ads', 'cms', 'crm', 'email', 'ledger', 'pay', 'quotes', 'wiki'] 8
# to sales: add ['crm', 'quotes'] remove ['ads', 'cms']
# to finance: add ['ledger', 'pay'] remove ['crm', 'quotes']
# desired:  ['email', 'ledger', 'pay', 'wiki'] 4
blocks.caption: Python. The wrong version edits access by adding; the right version computes what the HR record says Ana should hold, then applies the difference both ways. Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
Why the desired-state version works: it never asks "what should we add?". It asks "what should this person hold, given the authoritative record?", then makes reality match, removals included. Removal stops depending on someone remembering. This is the same idea as infrastructure as code (servers and settings described in files, with a tool making reality match them): declare the target, compute the diff.

Two practical wrinkles:

- **Handover periods.** A mover sometimes needs old access for a few weeks to train a replacement; Microsoft's access review documentation names exactly this case. Grant it as a **time-bound** exception with an end date, not as a permanent leftover.
- **People with no HR record.** Contractors, partners and guests often never appear in HR, so no mover or leaver event will ever fire for them. Give each one a named **sponsor** (an employee accountable for them) and an expiry date, and review them (lesson 4).

blocks.prompt: Under add-only provisioning, Ana ends up with 8 entitlements after two moves. Before reading on: besides the sheer number, what specific danger does the final add-only set contain?
blocks.reveal: Ana holds both **quotes** (from sales: set prices and discounts for customers) and **pay** (from finance: approve payments). Sales and payment approval are normally kept in different hands, so that one person cannot both arrange a deal and approve the money that moves on it, such as a refund or credit; lesson 6 calls a pair like this a toxic combination. Nobody ever *decided* to give Ana both; it accumulated. Creep is not only more access, it is combinations no single approval ever saw.

blocks.md: Compute access from the authoritative record (desired state) and apply the difference both ways. Movers are the riskiest event, because add-only processes never remove anything.

blocks.question: A company's provisioning tool grants the new department's role whenever someone changes department, and removes nothing. Which control from NIST SP 800-53 does this fail?
options: PS-5, which asks to review and confirm ongoing need for current access on reassignment and modify it
IA-5(7), which bans embedded static authenticators
AC-6(9), which asks to log privileged functions
PS-4, which covers exit interviews
blocks.explain: PS-5 Personnel Transfer is the mover control: on reassignment, review and confirm ongoing need for existing access and modify it to match. Add-only provisioning skips exactly that step. PS-4 is the leaver control.

blocks.question: A contractor was onboarded directly in three applications and never appears in the HR system. What is the most important control to add?
options: Give the contractor a longer password
Wait for the HR leaver event to remove their access
Assign a named employee sponsor and an expiry date, and include the accounts in reviews
Convert the contractor's accounts to shared accounts
blocks.explain: No HR record means no leaver event will ever fire. A sponsor makes a person accountable, and an expiry date makes removal the default. Shared accounts make accountability worse, not better.

lessons.title: Leavers: deprovisioning, SCIM and the Cash App download

blocks.md:
When someone leaves, everything that lets them act as the organisation must stop working: every account, every open session, every token and API key they created, every shared password they knew, every badge and hardware key. Anything left behind is access held by someone who no longer has a reason, a manager or a contract.

NIST SP 800-53 control **PS-4, Personnel Termination**, says that on termination the organisation disables system access within a defined time, terminates or revokes any authenticators and credentials associated with the person, and retrieves security-related property. Its guidance adds that timely action is essential when someone is terminated for cause, and that organisations may consider disabling the accounts *before* the person is told. AC-2 adds one item people forget: change the password of any shared or group account when a member leaves the group.

**Real case: Cash App Investing, 2022.** On 4 April 2022 Block, Inc., the company behind Cash App, filed a Form 8-K (the report US public companies file with the SEC, the Securities and Exchange Commission, to announce material events). It said a former employee had downloaded certain reports of its subsidiary Cash App Investing on 10 December 2021.

The filing is precise about the access problem: the employee had regular access to these reports as part of their past job responsibilities, but in this instance the reports were accessed without permission after their employment ended. The reports held customers' full names and brokerage account numbers, and for some customers portfolio value, holdings and one day of trading activity; Block said they did not include passwords, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, payment card or bank details. Cash App Investing contacted about **8.2 million** current and former customers and notified regulators and law enforcement.

blocks.title: One leaver, five systems: where the gap appears (illustration)

scenes.caption: Simplified illustration, not Cash App's actual timeline. At hour 0 HR records the termination. Until then every system shows the person as active.
Within an hour the IdP account is disabled and SCIM pushes the change to App A. New logins through single sign-on now fail.
Two gaps remain: a session opened before termination keeps working until it expires at hour 12, and the reports tool, with its own local login and no connector, stays active.
At hour 30 the former employee logs in to the reports tool directly. Nothing in single sign-on sees it. Only reconciliation (below) or the tool's own logs would.

blocks.md:
**SCIM** (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) is the IETF standard for pushing these changes into applications: RFC 7643 defines the user and group schema and RFC 7644 the protocol, both from September 2015. It is JSON over HTTPS. The IdP (identity provider) is the SCIM *client* and calls the application, which is the SCIM *service provider*.

A leaver can be handled two ways. **Deactivate**: set the user's `active` attribute to false. RFC 7643 leaves its exact meaning to the application, with the typical example that false means the account is suspended and cannot log in. **Delete**: send DELETE; RFC 7644 lets the application keep the record internally but requires it to return 404 for every later operation on that user. Deactivation is usually preferred first, because it keeps the account's history for investigations.

blocks.code:
PATCH /scim/v2/Users/2819c223-7f76-453a HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <token the app issued to the IdP>
Content-Type: application/scim+json

{"schemas": ["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"],
 "Operations": [{"op": "replace", "path": "active", "value": false}]}

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
blocks.caption: A SCIM deactivation as RFC 7644 defines a PATCH. The IdP sends it the moment HR marks the person as gone. What it does inside the app (block login, end sessions or neither) is up to the app.

blocks.md:
SCIM closes the front door of *connected* applications. It does not, by itself, touch:

- **Sessions and refresh tokens** already issued (the session lesson in the authentication course: a token works until it expires or is revoked server-side).
- **Personal API keys, OAuth grants and SSH keys** the person created, which live in the application, not the IdP.
- **Applications with no connector** and their local accounts, like the reports tool in the timeline.
- **Shared passwords** the person knew (AC-2 asks for them to be changed).

The safety net is **reconciliation**: regularly export every application's account list and compare it with the authoritative source.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date

HR = {  # authoritative source: employee id -> status, end date
    "E1001": ("active", None),
    "E1002": ("terminated", date(2026, 10, 2)),
    "E1003": ("terminated", date(2026, 11, 10)),
}
# accounts exported from one application (external id = HR id)
APP = [
    {"user": "ana", "ext": "E1001", "enabled": True,  "last_login": date(2026, 11, 12)},
    {"user": "raj", "ext": "E1002", "enabled": True,  "last_login": date(2026, 11, 9)},
    {"user": "kim", "ext": "E1003", "enabled": False, "last_login": date(2026, 11, 7)},
    {"user": "tmp-admin", "ext": None, "enabled": True, "last_login": date(2026, 6, 1)},
]

for a in APP:
    status, end = HR.get(a["ext"], (None, None))
    if status is None:
        print(f'{a["user"]:9} ORPHAN: no HR record, nobody will ever offboard it')
    elif status == "terminated" and a["enabled"]:
        late = a["last_login"] > end
        print(f'{a["user"]:9} LEAVER STILL ENABLED since {end}'
              + (f', logged in AFTER leaving ({a["last_login"]})' if late else ''))
    else:
        print(f'{a["user"]:9} ok')

# output:
# ana       ok
# raj       LEAVER STILL ENABLED since 2026-10-02, logged in AFTER leaving (2026-11-09)
# kim       ok
# tmp-admin ORPHAN: no HR record, nobody will ever offboard it
blocks.caption: Python. Reconciliation joins an application's accounts to HR records. It finds a leaver who is still enabled (and used the account after leaving) and an orphan account that matches nobody. Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**

- *Prevent*: drive leavers from HR; connect every application that holds sensitive data to SCIM or another connector; on termination also revoke sessions and refresh tokens, personal tokens and keys, and change shared secrets; for terminations for cause, disable first.
- *Detect*: alert on any successful login or data access by an identity whose HR status is terminated; reconcile disconnected applications at least weekly; watch bulk downloads by people who have resigned and are working their notice period.
- *Respond*: disable everything at once, preserve the application's logs, establish exactly what was accessed, and notify as the law requires, as Block did with regulators and customers.
Disabling the IdP account is not deprovisioning. It blocks the next single sign-on. Sessions already open, tokens already issued, local accounts and shared passwords all survive it.

blocks.question: Block's filing says the former employee had regular access to the reports in a past role, and used it after leaving. Which control most directly addresses that failure?
options: Stronger password rules for employees
Removing every entitlement, including in tools with local accounts, at termination, then reconciling to catch misses
Encrypting the reports at rest
Requiring employees to sign a non-disclosure agreement
blocks.explain: The access itself outlived the job. Complete deprovisioning, including applications outside single sign-on, and reconciliation to catch what was missed, address that directly. Encryption at rest does not stop an authorised account from reading data.

blocks.question: An application handles SCIM deactivation by setting active to false, which blocks new logins. What still needs to happen for a leaver?
options: Nothing: SCIM deactivation is complete deprovisioning
Delete the user's HR record
Send a second PATCH setting active to true and then false again
Revoke existing sessions, refresh tokens, personal API keys and OAuth grants, and change shared passwords they knew
blocks.explain: RFC 7643 lets each application define what active false means; commonly it only blocks login. Anything already issued keeps working until revoked, and shared secrets the person knew must be changed.

lessons.title: Access reviews and certification: asking again, and meaning it

blocks.md:
Lifecycle automation handles the events HR knows about. It cannot know that Ben no longer uses the export function, that a project ended, or that a guest finished their work. So, periodically, a person who understands the business is asked to look at who holds what and say yes or no again. That is an **access review**; when the reviewer formally attests to the result, it is called **certification** or **recertification**.

NIST SP 800-53 asks for this twice: **AC-2** says to review accounts for compliance with account management requirements at a set frequency, and **AC-6(7), Review of User Privileges**, says to review the privileges assigned to defined roles or classes of users to validate the need for them, and to remove privileges that are no longer needed.

**Real case: Twitter, July 2020.** The New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) investigated how attackers took over 130 Twitter accounts after phoning employees (the authentication course told the phishing half). Its report found that Twitter did limit access to its powerful internal tools, but **over 1,000 Twitter employees** still had access to them for job functions such as account support and content review. The report states that each user should have access only to the extent necessary for their job and that "Access should be recertified regularly, to account for changes in roles and responsibilities." Immediately after the attack, Twitter further limited the number of employees with access, even though that slowed some job functions.

With 1,000 people holding the tool, attackers only needed to fool a few of them.

Who reviews? Microsoft's access review product shows the usual choices: a **resource owner** (who knows what the application is for), the person's **manager** (who knows what the job is), named **specified reviewers**, or **self-review** (the user confirms they still need it, which is cheap but weak). Reviews can recur weekly, monthly, quarterly or annually.

A review produces a decision per **item** (one person, one entitlement): approve or deny. Decide in advance what a missing answer means. For privileged and sensitive access the safe default is removal, because "nobody answered" is not evidence that the access is needed. Denials must flow back into provisioning so the entitlement is actually removed, and the whole campaign produces evidence for auditors.

blocks.title: One review campaign from launch to evidence

scenes.caption: The campaign starts: the tool pulls who holds what from the application, plus last-used dates from its logs, and sends each reviewer their items.
The reviewer decides each item. Hints from usage data make the obvious denials quick: never used, or idle for months.
Denials become removals. A review whose denials are never applied changes nothing but paperwork.
The tool keeps who decided what and when, and proves removal happened. That is the fourth governance question answered.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date
TODAY = date(2026, 11, 13)

# one review item per (user, entitlement), with usage pulled from logs
items = [
    ("ana", "crm:export",    date(2026, 11, 10)),
    ("ben", "crm:export",    date(2026, 3, 2)),
    ("cy",  "admin-console", None),               # never used
    ("dee", "admin-console", date(2026, 11, 1)),
]

def recommend(last_used, stale_days=90):
    if last_used is None:
        return "REVOKE (never used)"
    idle = (TODAY - last_used).days
    return f"REVOKE (idle {idle} d)" if idle > stale_days else f"keep (used {idle} d ago)"

for user, ent, used in items:
    print(f"{user:4} {ent:14} {recommend(used)}")

# reviewer behaviour: (reviewer, items, approved, median seconds per item)
for who, n, ok, secs in [("lee", 212, 212, 2), ("mo", 40, 31, 45)]:
    flag = "  <- rubber stamp?" if ok == n and secs < 5 else ""
    print(f"{who}: approved {ok}/{n} ({ok/n:.0%}), {secs}s per item{flag}")

# output:
# ana  crm:export     keep (used 3 d ago)
# ben  crm:export     REVOKE (idle 256 d)
# cy   admin-console  REVOKE (never used)
# dee  admin-console  keep (used 12 d ago)
# lee: approved 212/212 (100%), 2s per item  <- rubber stamp?
# mo: approved 31/40 (78%), 45s per item
blocks.caption: Python. Usage data turns each item into a recommendation, and reviewer behaviour shows whether anyone is really looking. Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
The last two lines show the classic failure, **rubber-stamping**: a reviewer who approves every one of 212 items at two seconds each did not review anything. Reviews fail this way when reviewers get long lists of cryptic entitlement names with no context.

What makes reviews real:

- **Context**: show the reason each grant exists (the rule or request from lesson 1) and when it was last used.
- **Small, targeted campaigns**: review privileged and sensitive access often; review birthright access rarely or not at all, because rules already govern it.
- **Event-triggered reviews**: a mover event should trigger a review of the old department's access.
- **Measure the reviewers**: approval rates near 100% and seconds per item are signals to escalate, not to celebrate.
A completed review is not the same as a working control. 100% approved in two seconds per item is evidence that a form was filled in.

blocks.question: NYDFS found over 1,000 Twitter employees had access to internal tools that could take over any account. Which governance practice most directly reduces that exposure?
options: Annual security awareness training for all staff
Regular recertification of who needs the tools, with denials actually removed, plus fewer people holding them
A longer minimum password length
Moving the internal tools to a different domain name
blocks.explain: The exposure is the number of people holding a powerful entitlement. Recertification with removal shrinks it; NYDFS states access should be recertified regularly. Training helps against phishing but leaves 1,000 targets.

blocks.question: A quarterly review of the admin console finishes 100% complete. One reviewer approved 212 of 212 items in about 2 seconds each. What should happen next?
options: Nothing: the campaign completed on time
Delete the reviewer's own account
Treat those decisions as unreviewed: re-run them with usage context or a different reviewer, and follow up with the reviewer
Approve all items automatically next quarter to save time
blocks.explain: Completion is not quality. Uniform approval at two seconds an item suggests nobody judged the need, so the decisions provide no assurance. Re-review with context, and treat reviewer behaviour as a metric.

lessons.title: Role mining and role engineering: from a pile of grants to roles

blocks.md:
The access control course introduced RBAC (role-based access control): permissions go to roles, people go to roles. It also warned about **role explosion**, one role per combination of team, region and customer. Governance meets the opposite problem first: a company that has run for years on direct grants, with thousands of people each holding a slightly different pile of entitlements. Reviews of 50,000 individual grants are hopeless. Reviews of 40 well-understood roles are possible.

There are two ways to get roles:

- **Role engineering** (top down): start from job functions and ask owners what each job needs. NIST's RBAC project page describes the basic move: administrators determine which operations each job needs, then assign staff to the matching roles.
- **Role mining** (bottom up): start from who holds what today and look for groups of permissions that many people share.

In 2007 Jaideep Vaidya, Vijayalakshmi Atluri and Qi Guo, researchers at Rutgers University, defined the **role mining problem** at SACMAT (the Association for Computing Machinery's Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies): discover an optimal set of roles from existing user permissions, meaning the smallest set of roles that exactly reproduces the current user-permission table. They proved it is **NP-complete** by reducing the known set basis problem to it. NP-complete means no known algorithm solves every instance quickly, so real tools use heuristics: they generate candidate roles and pick good ones greedily.

The input is a matrix: one row per user, one column per permission, a 1 where the user holds it. Roles show up as blocks of 1s that many rows share.

blocks.title: Six users, seven permissions: what a miner sees

scenes.caption: The raw table: 26 grants across 6 users. Nobody wrote down why any of them exist.
Candidate role 1: ledger, mail, pay, wiki, held in full by dee, eli and fay. Assigning it explains 12 grants at once.
Candidate role 2: crm, mail, quotes, wiki, held by ana, ben and cy. Another 12 grants explained.
Two grants fit no role: cy's ledger and fay's db. These exceptions are the most interesting output of the whole exercise.

blocks.code:
from itertools import combinations
UP = {  # user -> permissions they hold today
    "ana": {"mail", "wiki", "crm", "quotes"},
    "ben": {"mail", "wiki", "crm", "quotes"},
    "cy":  {"mail", "wiki", "crm", "quotes", "ledger"},
    "dee": {"mail", "wiki", "ledger", "pay"},
    "eli": {"mail", "wiki", "ledger", "pay"},
    "fay": {"mail", "wiki", "ledger", "pay", "db"},
}
# candidate roles: every user's set and every pairwise intersection
cands = {frozenset(s) for s in UP.values()}
cands |= {frozenset(a & b) for a, b in combinations(UP.values(), 2) if a & b}

todo = {(u, p) for u, ps in UP.items() for p in ps}   # pairs to explain
roles = []
while todo:
    # a role may go only to users who already hold ALL of its permissions
    def gain(r):
        return sum((u, p) in todo for u, ps in UP.items() if r <= ps for p in r)
    best = max(cands, key=lambda r: (gain(r), len(r), sorted(r)))
    if gain(best) < 4:            # too little left to explain: stop
        break
    users = [u for u, ps in UP.items() if best <= ps]
    roles.append((sorted(best), users))
    todo -= {(u, p) for u in users for p in best}

for i, (perms, users) in enumerate(roles, 1):
    print(f"role {i}: {perms} -> {users}")
print("left as direct grants:", sorted(todo))

# output:
# role 1: ['ledger', 'mail', 'pay', 'wiki'] -> ['dee', 'eli', 'fay']
# role 2: ['crm', 'mail', 'quotes', 'wiki'] -> ['ana', 'ben', 'cy']
# left as direct grants: [('cy', 'ledger'), ('fay', 'db')]
blocks.caption: Python. A greedy miner: candidates are users' own sets and pairwise intersections; it repeatedly picks the candidate that explains the most remaining grants. Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
Two roles plus two exceptions now describe 26 grants. Notice what the miner did *not* do: it never gave a role to someone who lacked any of its permissions (`r <= ps`), so mining never adds access. But it also cannot tell good access from bad. It found what exists.

That is why the exceptions matter. Is cy's ledger access a real need, or a leftover from a move (lesson 2)? Does fay need the database? Mining turns 26 unexplained grants into two questions an owner can answer in a minute. The mined roles also need an owner's sign-off before they become official, because they encode today's reality, mistakes included. In practice the two methods meet in the middle: mine candidates, then engineer them with the business.

blocks.prompt: Suppose ana and ben also held ledger, left over from earlier jobs in finance, just like cy. Re-run the same miner. What do you expect it to do with ledger?
blocks.reveal:
It bakes the leftover into the roles. Running the script with that change gives:

```
role 1: ['ledger', 'mail', 'wiki'] -> ['ana', 'ben', 'cy', 'dee', 'eli', 'fay']
role 2: ['crm', 'ledger', 'mail', 'quotes', 'wiki'] -> ['ana', 'ben', 'cy']
left as direct grants: [('dee', 'pay'), ('eli', 'pay'), ('fay', 'db'), ('fay', 'pay')]
```

Ledger is now part of the *sales* role. Once that role is approved, every future sales joiner gets ledger by design. The real finance role also vanishes: pay is left as three direct grants. Mining finds patterns, including the pattern of a common mistake, so owners must validate roles before adopting them.

blocks.md: Role mining compresses what exists; it does not judge it. Use it to find candidate roles and, above all, the exceptions, then have owners confirm each role before it governs new joiners.

blocks.question: Why do role-mining tools use heuristics such as greedy selection instead of always finding the minimal set of roles?
options: Because minimal role sets are always insecure
Because Vaidya, Atluri and Guo showed the role mining problem is NP-complete, so exact solutions do not scale
Because RBAC forbids more than ten roles
Because the user-permission matrix is secret
blocks.explain: The 2007 SACMAT paper proved RMP NP-complete by reduction from the set basis problem. Large real matrices therefore need approximate methods.

blocks.question: A mined role for the support team includes the permission to delete customer accounts, because most support staff happen to hold it today. What should happen before the role is adopted?
options: Adopt it: mining reflects what people use
Remove the support team from RBAC entirely
The role owner checks each permission against the job; holding something widely is not evidence it is needed
Split the role so each person has a personal role
blocks.explain: Mining reproduces current access, including widespread over-provisioning. An owner must validate the role. Personal roles would recreate the original mess.

lessons.title: Separation of duties: toxic combinations and two-person control

blocks.md:
Some tasks are safe only when two different people do the parts. If one person can create a new supplier in the finance system *and* approve payments, they can invent a supplier and pay it. Neither permission is dangerous alone; the pair is. Practitioners call such pairs **toxic combinations**.

NIST SP 800-53 control **AC-5, Separation of Duties**, asks organisations to identify the duties that must be separated and to define access to support that. Its guidance explains the purpose: separation addresses the potential for abuse of authorised privileges and reduces the risk of malicious activity *without collusion*, meaning one person can no longer do it alone; two would have to conspire. The guidance gives a security example too: security staff who administer access control should not also administer the audit functions that would record their actions.

Ravi Sandhu, David Ferraiolo and Richard Kuhn, the researchers behind the NIST RBAC model, describe separation of duties (SOD) as a time-honoured technique, practised long before computers, that spreads the responsibility and authority for an action over multiple users. Their model names two kinds:

- **Static SOD**: enforced at assignment time. Two conflicting roles may never be assigned to the same user.
- **Dynamic SOD**: enforced at activation time. A user may hold both roles but may not use both in the same session.

Static SOD is simpler to reason about and to audit. Dynamic SOD suits small teams where people must cover for each other, at the cost of needing the system to track sessions carefully.

blocks.title: One person or two: the supplier payment path

scenes.caption: Raj holds both permissions. Raj can create a fake supplier and approve its invoice. Nothing technical stops it, and nobody else is involved.
Split the duties: Raj creates suppliers, Mo approves payments. A fake supplier now needs Mo to approve its payment, so fraud needs collusion.

AC-5's own example: whoever administers access control should not also administer the audit log. Applied here, the log of payment approvals has a separate administrator, so a misused approval leaves a record the approver cannot erase.

blocks.code:
# Conflicting pairs: holding both lets one person finish a risky task alone
SOD_RULES = [
    ("vendor:create",    "payment:approve", "could pay a fake vendor"),
    ("user:grant-admin", "audit-log:delete", "could cover own tracks"),
    ("code:merge",       "deploy:prod-approve", "could ship unreviewed code"),
]
HOLDINGS = {
    "ana": {"vendor:create", "invoice:view"},
    "raj": {"vendor:create", "payment:approve"},     # existing violation
    "sam": {"user:grant-admin"},
}

def conflicts(perms):
    return [(a, b, why) for a, b, why in SOD_RULES if a in perms and b in perms]

# detective: scan what people already hold
for user, perms in HOLDINGS.items():
    for a, b, why in conflicts(perms):
        print(f"VIOLATION {user}: {a} + {b} ({why})")

# preventive: check a request BEFORE granting it
def request(user, perm):
    clash = conflicts(HOLDINGS[user] | {perm})
    if clash:
        a, b, _ = clash[0]
        return f"DENY {user} {perm}: conflicts with {b if perm == a else a}"
    HOLDINGS[user].add(perm)
    return f"GRANT {user} {perm}"

print(request("ana", "payment:approve"))
print(request("sam", "audit-log:delete"))
print(request("sam", "invoice:view"))

# output:
# VIOLATION raj: vendor:create + payment:approve (could pay a fake vendor)
# DENY ana payment:approve: conflicts with vendor:create
# DENY sam audit-log:delete: conflicts with user:grant-admin
# GRANT sam invoice:view
blocks.caption: Python. The same rule list runs two ways: detective (scan what people already hold) and preventive (check a request before granting it). Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
Both modes matter. **Preventive** checks stop new violations at request time, as in the last three lines. **Detective** scans find violations that already exist, from before the rules were written or from grants made outside the request process, like Raj's.

Sometimes a violation cannot be removed: a three-person company has nobody else to approve payments. Then you add a **mitigating control** and write it down: someone outside the duty reviews every payment report weekly, or the bank requires a second signature above a threshold.

For the most dangerous actions, the strongest form is **two-person control**: the action itself needs two people at the time it happens. The NYDFS report on Twitter suggests exactly this for high-risk functions, requiring approval by a second employee before the action, so compromising one employee's access is not enough. Microsoft's privileged access guidance likewise recommends a second person in business-critical workflows to raise the cost of insider collusion.

Separation of duties makes misuse require collusion. Write the conflicting pairs down, check requests against them (preventive), scan existing access (detective), and add a mitigating control wherever a split is impossible.

blocks.question: A user may hold both the 'payment requester' and 'payment approver' roles, but the system refuses to let them approve a payment in a session where they requested it. Which kind of separation of duties is this?
options: Static, because it is decided when roles are assigned
Dynamic, because it is enforced when roles are used in a session
Neither: holding both roles always violates SOD
Discretionary access control
blocks.explain: Sandhu, Ferraiolo and Kuhn distinguish static SOD (based on user-role assignment) from dynamic SOD (based on role activation). Holding both but not using both together is dynamic.

blocks.question: Why does AC-5's guidance say people who administer access control should not also administer audit functions?
options: Because audit logs are too large for one team
Because someone who grants themselves access could otherwise also erase the record of doing so
Because audit tools need a different operating system
Because access administrators are always contractors
blocks.explain: Separating the two means misuse of access administration still leaves a record that the same person cannot remove. One person would need both duties, or a colluder, to hide it.

lessons.title: Privileged access: why admin rights differ, and the Snowden case

blocks.md:
Most accounts can damage what one person can see. A few can damage everything: the domain administrator who can reset any password, the cloud administrator who can delete every account, the database administrator who can read every row, the person who manages the backup system. NIST's glossary defines a **privileged account** as a system account with the authorizations of a privileged user, and SP 800-53 **AC-6(5)** says to restrict privileged accounts to specific named personnel or roles.

Privileged access is not only people. A service account that the backup software uses to read every server is privileged too (lesson 12). So is anyone who can change *who* is privileged: whoever administers the PAM tool, the identity provider or the group that grants admin rights.

Three rules follow from the NIST controls:

- **Fewer.** Count privileged accounts and drive the number down (AC-6(5)).
- **Separate.** **AC-6(2)** says users with privileged accounts use non-privileged accounts for non-security work. The administrator reads email as ana, and administers as a separate ana-admin account, so a phishing email lands on an account with no admin rights.
- **Scrutinised.** NIST SP 800-207, the zero trust architecture standard, says users with special privileges, such as developers or system administrators, require additional scrutiny when being assigned attributes or roles, and that logs and audit actions should be used to identify their access behaviour patterns.

The biggest structural problem is **standing privilege**: rights that are on all the time, whether or not anyone is using them. A stolen admin password is useful at 03:00 on a Sunday because the rights behind it never switch off.

blocks.title: Hours per week that one admin's rights are live

scenes.caption: Standing privilege is live all 168 hours of the week, whatever the admin does. Just-in-time rights are live only during activations: at 3 activations of 2 hours, 6 hours.
Longer windows erode the benefit: at 8 hours per activation and 20 activations, rights are live 160 of 168 hours. Just-in-time access with day-long windows is standing privilege with extra steps.
Simplified model: it counts exposure time only. Lessons 10 and 11 add what also matters, such as which device the session runs on and who approved it.

blocks.code:
HOURS_PER_WEEK = 24 * 7
admins = 12

standing = admins * HOURS_PER_WEEK            # admin rights live all week
activations, hours_each = 3, 2                # JIT: 3 windows of 2 h per admin
jit = admins * activations * hours_each

print("standing admin-hours/week:", standing)
print("JIT admin-hours/week:     ", jit)
print(f"reduction: {1 - jit / standing:.1%}")
# chance a stolen admin session lands inside a live window, if theft
# time is uniform over the week (a simplification)
print(f"P(window open at a random hour): {activations * hours_each / HOURS_PER_WEEK:.1%}")

# output:
# standing admin-hours/week: 2016
# JIT admin-hours/week:      72
# reduction: 96.4%
# P(window open at a random hour): 3.6%
blocks.caption: Python. Twelve admins with standing rights versus three 2-hour activations each. The last line assumes theft happens at a uniformly random hour, a deliberate simplification. Output is from running the script.

blocks.md:
**Real case: Edward Snowden and the NSA, 2013.** In June 2013 Edward Snowden, then a contractor for the NSA (US National Security Agency), carried out what the House committee calls the largest and most damaging public release of classified information in US intelligence history. The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (HPSCI) reviewed the case for two years. Its unclassified summary (September 2016) says Snowden removed more than 1.5 million classified documents from NSA networks.

For identity governance, three of the committee's findings matter. Snowden obtained colleagues' security credentials through misleading means; **abused their access as a systems administrator** to search co-workers' personal network drives; and began mass downloading two weeks after being reprimanded in a workplace dispute in 2012. Its [highlights document](https://intelligence.house.gov/uploadedfiles/snowden_report_highlights.pdf) dates the start of the mass downloading to 12 July 2012, eight months before the March 2013 testimony Snowden later called the breaking point.

What changed afterwards was a privileged access programme. A Department of Defense Inspector General audit (report DODIG-2016-129, August 2016, released in redacted form in 2017) looked at seven of NSA's **Secure-the-Net** initiatives, aimed at malicious insiders. According to Nextgov (a US government tech news site), NSA had implemented two-person access controls for data centres and machine rooms and two-stage authentication for administrators (not yet for all high-level ones), but had not fully implemented technology to oversee privileged user activity, nor reduced the number of privileged users and authorised data transfer agents. The inspector general recommended automated, technology-based monitoring of all administrators. The HPSCI summary, a month later, said NSA had yet to effectively implement its post-Snowden security improvements.

Map that to this course: fewer administrators (AC-6(5)), no credential sharing, two-person control (lesson 6), monitored privileged sessions (lesson 9) and someone other than the administrators reading those logs.

Administrators are trusted to touch everything, so their misuse looks like their job. Detection only works if privileged activity is logged somewhere the administrator cannot edit, and reviewed by someone else (AC-5 and AC-6(9), log the use of privileged functions).

blocks.question: Ana is a domain administrator who also reads email and browses the web all day on the same account. Which NIST control does this break, and why does it matter?
options: AC-6(2): privileged users should use a non-privileged account for non-security work, so a phishing email does not land on an admin account
PS-4: Ana has not left the company
AC-2(3): Ana's account is not dormant
IA-5(7): there is no embedded password
blocks.explain: AC-6(2) separates everyday work from admin work. If the account that opens attachments is also a domain admin, any malware it runs starts with domain admin rights.

blocks.question: The DoD Inspector General audit of NSA's post-Snowden initiatives found which privileged-access measures not fully implemented?
options: Two-person access controls for data centres and machine rooms
Encryption of all classified documents at rest
Technology to oversee privileged user activity, and reducing the number of privileged users and data transfer agents
Background checks for all contractors
blocks.explain: Per the redacted DODIG-2016-129 as reported by Nextgov, two-person access to data centres and machine rooms was implemented; monitoring privileged users and shrinking their numbers were not. (Two-stage authentication was installed for administrators but, per the same report, not yet fully for high-level administrators.)

lessons.title: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script

blocks.md:
Imagine 400 servers, each with a root password, plus database admin passwords, network device passwords and cloud break-glass keys. Before PAM, these lived in spreadsheets, scripts and people's memories, rarely changed, and were known by everyone who had ever needed them once.

A **PAM vault** takes all of them into one encrypted store and changes how people use them. Microsoft's guidance on privileged access lists what PAM solutions typically do: simplify service account management and password rotation (which it calls critically important), provide workflows for just-in-time access, and record and monitor administrative sessions.

The core workflow is **check-out and check-in**:

1. Ana asks the vault for the root password of db1, citing a change ticket.
2. Policy decides: automatic for low-risk targets, or an approver must agree.
3. The vault releases the credential for a fixed window, or better, never shows it: it **injects** it into a session it opens for Ana (session brokering, next lesson).
4. When Ana checks in, or the window ends, the vault **rotates** the password. Whatever Ana saw is now useless.

The strongest form removes long-lived passwords entirely. The database secrets engine of HashiCorp Vault (a widely used secrets management tool) generates **dynamic credentials**: a new database user, created on request, with a lease (a time to live; the role in the docs example sets a default of one hour and a maximum of 24), revoked by Vault when the lease expires. Each service gets its own credentials, so the database username in a log points to one client.

scenes.caption: Ana requests access to db1 and names the change ticket. Nobody holds the root password; only the vault does.
Policy requires approval for production databases. A second person agrees, and the decision is logged with the ticket.
The vault logs in to db1 on Ana's behalf and hands Ana the session, not the password. The session is recorded.
At check-in, or when 2 hours end, the vault sets a new random password on db1. Any copy that leaked during the window is dead.

blocks.code:
$ vault read database/creds/my-role
Key                Value
---                -----
lease_id           database/creds/my-role/2f6a614c-4aa2-7b19-24b9-ad944a8d4de6
lease_duration     1h
lease_renewable    true
password           FSREZ1S0kFsZtLat-y94
username           v-vaultuser-e2978cd0-ugp7iqI2hdlff5hfjylJ-1602537260
blocks.caption: The example output from HashiCorp's database secrets engine documentation (not run here). The username is generated per request and the lease says when Vault will revoke it.

blocks.md:
A vault concentrates risk as well as control. Microsoft's guidance puts it plainly: PIM (privileged identity management) and PAM solutions typically store the credentials for most or all privileged roles in the organisation, which makes them a highly lucrative target. Whoever administers the vault administers everything in it.

**Real case: Uber, September 2022.** The authentication course covered how the attacker got in: a contractor's stolen password plus repeated MFA push prompts until one was accepted. What happened next is a PAM lesson. The Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB, a US board, disbanded in January 2025, that reviewed major cyber incidents) report on Lapsus$ and related groups lists, among the ways these attackers escalated, "privileged credentials embedded in a PowerShell script, stored on a misconfigured network share", citing an analysis by CyberArk, a PAM vendor. CyberArk's account is that the share was readable by ordinary staff and the script held hard-coded administrator credentials for Uber's PAM system, from which the attacker could reach further secrets.

Uber's own update did not describe the script. It said the attacker reached other employee accounts that gave elevated permissions to tools including G-Suite and Slack, accessed an internal finance tool and Uber's dashboard on HackerOne (its bug bounty platform), and that Uber rotated keys to many internal services and locked down its codebase. So treat the script details as reported by the CSRB and CyberArk, not confirmed by Uber.

The pattern has a MITRE ATT&CK entry, **T1552.001, Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files**, and a NIST control, **IA-5(7)**: ensure that unencrypted static authenticators are not embedded in applications or other forms of static storage.

blocks.code:
# VULNERABLE: the pattern the Uber reports describe. A script on a share
# that ordinary staff can read, holding a PAM administrator password.
$user = "pam-admin"
$pass = ConvertTo-SecureString "Winter-2019!" -AsPlainText -Force
$cred = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential($user, $pass)
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://pam.corp.example/api/report" -Credential $cred

# FIXED: no secret in the file. The task runs as its own least-privilege
# identity, reads a credential scoped to read-only reporting from a vault
# at run time, and the vault rotates it.
$cred = Get-Secret -Name "pam-report-reader" -Vault "CorpVault"
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://pam.corp.example/api/report" -Credential $cred
blocks.caption: PowerShell (Microsoft's scripting shell), not run here. The fix removes the secret from storage (IA-5(7)) and the admin rights from the job. Get-Secret comes from Microsoft's SecretManagement module, feature complete and archived; an identity needing no stored secret is better still.

blocks.md:
Why the fix works: the file now contains nothing worth stealing. The secret it fetches is scoped to read-only reporting, so even someone who runs the script gets a report, not the keys to the vault. And because the vault rotates it, a copy taken today expires.

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent*: scan shares and repositories for secrets; phishing-resistant MFA and a dedicated workstation (lesson 10) for vault administrators; no human or script holds vault admin rights by default.
- *Detect*: alert on logins to the vault's admin console, on bulk secret retrieval, and on secrets retrieved by identities that never did so before.
- *Respond*: if the vault is touched, assume every secret in it is exposed and rotate all of them, as Uber rotated keys across many internal services.

A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

blocks.question: Why does rotating a privileged password at check-in matter even if the admin was fully trusted?
options: It makes the password longer
Any copy that leaked during the window, from a keylogger, a screenshot or a note, stops working
It is required for the session recording to start
It deletes the admin's account
blocks.explain: Rotation limits the life of every copy. The admin's trustworthiness does not protect against malware on their device or a password pasted somewhere it should not be.

blocks.question: After the Uber pattern, a team moves the PAM admin password from a script into an environment variable on the same file server. What is still wrong?
options: Nothing: environment variables are encrypted
PowerShell cannot read environment variables
The password is now too short
A static PAM admin secret is still stored where people and processes on that server can read it, and the job still runs with vault admin rights
blocks.explain: Moving a static secret to another readable place does not satisfy IA-5(7)'s intent, and the job still holds far more privilege than reporting needs. Remove the secret and the excess privilege.

lessons.title: Bastions, jump hosts and session brokering

blocks.md:
If every administrator can reach every server directly, from any laptop, then every laptop is a path to every server, and there is no single place to watch admin traffic. The classic fix is to funnel administration through one guarded doorway.

A **jump server** (also **jump host**) is a machine administrators connect to first, and only from it onward to the servers they manage; the servers accept admin connections only from it. NIST's glossary, quoting the US Committee on National Security Systems, defines a **bastion host** as a special purpose computer on a network specifically designed and configured to withstand attacks. In practice the two names are used for the same role: the one hardened, exposed entry point for administration.

blocks.title: Funnelling admin access through one doorway

scenes.caption: Before: the laptop reaches db1 directly. Any laptop could, so the servers' firewalls cannot tell admin traffic from an intruder's.
After: servers accept SSH only from the bastion's address. One door to harden, patch and require MFA at.
One door is also one place to log and record every privileged session, which AC-17(4) and AC-6(9) ask for.
The catch: the bastion now sees every admin session. If admins type passwords or park keys on it, compromising it yields all of them.

blocks.md: That last scene is Microsoft's main warning about such **intermediaries**. Its guidance calls jump servers used by administrators a host where many or all sensitive sessions pass through, enabling attackers to use standard credential-theft tools to steal and reuse credentials; VPNs and jump servers are frequently exposed and neglected, and an attacker needs only one unpatched service. The rule it states for every intermediary: it is a link in the chain and must sustain or improve the security of the session, so it needs secure configuration, rapid patching, endpoint detection and response (EDR), and strict control over who administers the intermediary itself.

Design so the bastion does not *hold* secrets. With SSH this is easy. `ssh -J bastion db1` (the ProxyJump option) makes an SSH connection to the bastion and then a TCP forwarding through it, so the end-to-end SSH session runs from the laptop to db1 and the private key never leaves the laptop. The ssh manual warns that the older habit, **agent forwarding** (`ssh -A`), lets anyone who can bypass file permissions on the remote host use your loaded keys, and suggests a jump host as the safer alternative.

blocks.code:
# ~/.ssh/config on the admin workstation
Host bastion
    HostName bastion.corp.example
    User ana

Host db1
    HostName 10.20.0.15
    User db-admin
    ProxyJump bastion        # same as: ssh -J bastion db1
    ForwardAgent no          # never expose the agent to hosts on the way

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config on db1: trust the admin CA, not individual keys
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/admin_ca.pub
AuthorizedPrincipalsFile /etc/ssh/principals/%u   # db-admin -> "db-admin"
RevokedKeys /etc/ssh/revoked.krl
blocks.caption: OpenSSH configuration. The client hops through the bastion without leaving keys on it; the server accepts only certificates from the admin CA whose principals match. Options are as documented in the OpenSSH manual pages.

blocks.md:
**Short-lived certificates instead of standing keys.** A plain SSH key in `authorized_keys` is standing privilege: it works until someone remembers to remove it. OpenSSH can instead trust a **certificate authority** (CA): `TrustedUserCAKeys` lists CA keys whose certificates sshd accepts, and `AuthorizedPrincipalsFile` lists the principal names, one of which must appear in the certificate. The CA signs a user's public key with a list of principals (roles), a validity window and options. The ssh-keygen manual notes that the key identifier given with `-I` is logged by the server whenever the certificate is used, so naming it after the change ticket links every login to a reason.

Below, the CA gives Ana a one-hour certificate for the `db-admin` principal with agent, port and X11 (the Unix graphical display system) forwarding off (real output from OpenSSH 10.3). The start is backdated to tolerate poorly synchronised clocks: ssh-keygen's source subtracts 59 seconds and rounds down to the minute, so here it starts 1 minute 45 seconds early.

blocks.code:
$ ssh-keygen -s admin_ca -I ana-CHG-1042 -n db-admin -z 1042 -V +1h \
      -O no-agent-forwarding -O no-port-forwarding -O no-x11-forwarding ana.pub
Signed user key ana-cert.pub: id "ana-CHG-1042" serial 1042 for db-admin valid from 2026-11-13T23:14:00 to 2026-11-14T00:15:45

$ ssh-keygen -L -f ana-cert.pub
ana-cert.pub:
        Type: ssh-ed25519-cert-v01@openssh.com user certificate
        Public key: ED25519-CERT SHA256:nzzsX6bfPnQyKhnprbdAjM8f+dVRnQEeUCnpcbhtbG4
        Signing CA: ED25519 SHA256:e73H7hTeKSfLbDmtD6rLbVIqpTaQP6tJDavsbCjUs+I (using ssh-ed25519)
        Key ID: "ana-CHG-1042"
        Serial: 1042
        Valid: from 2026-11-13T23:14:00 to 2026-11-14T00:15:45
        Principals:
                db-admin
        Critical Options: (none)
        Extensions:
                permit-pty
                permit-user-rc
blocks.caption: Real output. In a PAM or just-in-time system, the CA signing step runs only after the request is approved (lesson 11), so the approval and the credential are the same event. To cut a certificate off early, list it in the RevokedKeys file.

blocks.md:
**Session brokering** goes one step further. A PAM proxy terminates the admin's connection, opens a second connection to the target using a credential the admin never sees (injection, lesson 8), and records the session: keystrokes, commands, or screen video for RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol). NIST SP 800-53 **AC-17(4)** asks that privileged commands over remote access be authorised only in a format that provides assessable evidence, and **AC-6(9)** asks to log the execution of privileged functions. A recording that nobody can edit and somebody actually samples is that evidence.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: servers accept admin protocols only from the bastion or broker; no passwords or keys stored on it; MFA at the bastion; patch it first. *Detect*: any admin login to a server from a source that is not the bastion is a high-severity alert; certificate key IDs in sshd logs that match no approved ticket. *Respond*: revoke the CA's trust or add certificates to the revocation list, and rotate anything that passed through a compromised intermediary.

blocks.question: Why is `ssh -J bastion db1` safer than logging in to the bastion and then running `ssh -A` onward?
options: Because -J uses a stronger cipher
Because with -J the end-to-end session runs from the laptop and keys stay there, while -A lets anyone who controls the bastion use the forwarded agent's keys
Because -J disables logging on the bastion
Because -A only works with passwords
blocks.explain: The ssh manual says agent forwarding lets users who can bypass file permissions on the remote host use the local agent, and names a jump host (-J) as the safer alternative.

blocks.question: A company adds a jump server and requires all admin RDP to pass through it. Admins type their domain admin passwords into RDP sessions launched from the jump server. What has the company created?
options: A host where every admin credential passes through, which attackers will target with credential-theft tools
A complete privileged access solution
A network that no longer needs patching
A way to make domain admin passwords expire
blocks.explain: Microsoft's guidance warns exactly about this: jump servers where many sensitive sessions pass let attackers steal and reuse credentials. Keep secrets off the intermediary and protect it as a privileged system.

lessons.title: Privileged access workstations and the clean source rule

blocks.md:
A vault, a bastion and a one-hour certificate all assume the admin's own computer is trustworthy. If Ana's laptop runs an infostealer (malware that copies passwords, cookies and tokens), the attacker sees whatever Ana sees, and can act in Ana's sessions while Ana is logged in. Microsoft calls the rule behind this the **clean source principle**: the security of a session is limited by the security of the device it starts from. Its guidance says an attacker with control of the device can impersonate users on it or steal their credentials, undermining assurances on the account, on intermediaries like jump servers, and on the resources.

Microsoft's own PAM guidance is blunt about the limit: PAM capabilities mitigate some attacks but do not address device compromise; vendors who sell PAM as a silver bullet for device risk are, in Microsoft's incident experience, wrong.

A **privileged access workstation** (PAW) is Microsoft's name for a computer used only for privileged work. Its guidance defines three device levels:

- **Enterprise**: managed, with anti-malware and EDR; users can browse the web and install software.
- **Specialized**: users are not local administrators of their machine and can run only applications installed by IT.
- **Privileged (PAW)**: the highest level. It blocks the most common phishing vectors, email and general web browsing; web traffic is limited to an allowlist of admin sites; applications are controlled; disks are encrypted. Admins get a second, ordinary device for email and the web.

Microsoft's emergency access guidance (lesson 11) also says the people allowed to use break-glass accounts should do so from a PAW or a similar designated secure workstation.

Where does a PAW fit? Microsoft's **enterprise access model** sorts systems into planes: the **control plane** (identity systems that decide access for everything, "Tier 0" in Microsoft's older tier model for Active Directory, the Windows directory service), the **management plane** (enterprise-wide IT management) and the **data and workload plane** (applications and data). Its rule is to **enforce hierarchy**: prevent control of higher planes from lower planes. A control-plane admin working from an ordinary laptop breaks that rule, because the laptop sits in the lowest plane.

Zero trust gives the vocabulary to design the whole admin path. NIST SP 800-207 defines a **policy engine** (PE), which makes the decision to grant, deny or revoke; a **policy administrator** (PA), which executes it by setting up or shutting down the path and generating any session-specific credential; and a **policy enforcement point** (PEP), which enables, monitors and terminates the connection. Together PE and PA play the role of the policy decision point (PDP) from the access control course.

The policy administrator carries out the decision: it issues a one-hour certificate and opens the path at the PEP. The session reaches the server.
The same request from Ana's email laptop fails the device check. Same person, same approval, wrong source: denied.
